name: Platform Adoption Essentials
description: The Platform Adoption Kernel establishes the universal foundation for platform transformations, organized into the three Areas of Concern.

focuses.name: Value
focuses.description: Focuses on business justification, financial management, and organizational alignment.

focuses.name: Solution
focuses.description: Encapsulates the design, provisioning, optimization, and the hosted items running on the platform foundation.

focuses.name: Endeavor
focuses.description: Governs the execution of the transformation, encompassing people, processes, and policies.

alphas.name: Opportunity
alphas.description: The foundational business drivers dictating the platform transformation.

states.name: Initiated
states.description: The desire to adopt a platform is identified.

states.name: Determined
states.description: The value and parameters of the platform are quantified.

states.name: Value Established
states.description: The platform's value is accepted by sponsors.

states.name: Viable
states.description: The business case demonstrates a viable return.

states.name: Addressed
states.description: The opportunity is actively being addressed by the platform.

states.name: Benefit Accrued
states.description: The expected benefits are being consistently realized.

alphas.name: Platform Value And Economics
alphas.description: The financial and outcome-based justification and accounting for the platform.

states.name: Modeled
states.description: Financial needs and potential values are recognized.

states.name: Allocated
states.description: Costs and benefits are logically modeled.

states.name: Sustained
states.description: The economic model is approved.

alphas.name: Stakeholders
alphas.description: The individuals, groups, or organizations affected by, or able to affect, the platform.

states.name: Recognized
states.description: Key stakeholders are identified.

states.name: Represented
states.description: Stakeholder representatives are designated.

states.name: Involved
states.description: Stakeholders actively participate.

states.name: In Agreement
states.description: Stakeholder expectations are aligned.

states.name: Satisfied for Deployment
states.description: Stakeholders approve deployment.

states.name: Satisfied in Use
states.description: Stakeholders are satisfied with the operational platform.

alphas.name: Requirements
alphas.description: The capabilities, features, and constraints the platform must satisfy.

states.name: Conceived
states.description: The need for a specific asset is identified.

states.name: Bounded
states.description: The scope of the requirements is defined.

states.name: Coherent
states.description: Requirements are clear, consistent, and logical.

states.name: Acceptable
states.description: Stakeholders agree the requirements meet their needs.

states.name: Addressed
states.description: The platform satisfies the established requirements.

states.name: Fulfilled
states.description: All requirements are successfully delivered and operational.

alphas.name: Platform
alphas.description: The unified system of assets and interfaces provided to consumers.

states.name: Architecture Selected
states.description: The foundational structure is chosen.

states.name: Baselined
states.description: Core capabilities are established.

states.name: Provisioned
states.description: The platform can be consumed.

states.name: Ready
states.description: The platform is fully operational.

states.name: Hosting Assets
states.description: The platform is actively supporting workloads.

states.name: Evolving
states.description: The platform is decommissioned.

alphas.name: Platform Consumption Interface
alphas.description: The means by which consumers interact with and consume platform assets.

states.name: Envisioned
states.description: The desired interface is conceptualized.

states.name: Scoped
states.description: Interface capabilities are defined.

states.name: Available
states.description: The interface is accessible.

states.name: Self Service
states.description: Consumers can independently use the interface.

states.name: Optimized
states.description: The interface provides a frictionless experience.

alphas.name: Platform Asset
alphas.description: The individual services, tools, or resources that constitute the platform.

states.name: Identified
states.description: The need for a specific asset is identified.

states.name: Specified
states.description: Asset requirements are detailed.

states.name: Provisioned
states.description: The asset is created or acquired.

states.name: Integrated
states.description: The asset works within the broader platform.

states.name: Operational
states.description: The asset is in active use.

states.name: Value Yielding
states.description: The asset is decommissioned.

alphas.name: Work
alphas.description: The activities required to build, operate, and maintain the platform.

states.name: Initiated
states.description: Work is requested.

states.name: Prepared
states.description: Work is ready to begin.

states.name: Started
states.description: Work is in progress.

states.name: Under Control
states.description: Work is proceeding predictably.

states.name: Concluded
states.description: Work is finished.

states.name: Closed
states.description: All work activities are officially complete.

alphas.name: Team
alphas.description: The group of individuals responsible for the platform's success.

states.name: Seeded
states.description: Initial team members are identified.

states.name: Formed
states.description: The team structure is established.

states.name: Collaborating
states.description: Team members work together effectively.

states.name: Performing
states.description: The team consistently delivers value.

states.name: Adjourned
states.description: The team is disbanded or repurposed.

alphas.name: Way Of Working
alphas.description: The tailored set of practices, tools, operational workflows, and industry alignments used by a team.

states.name: Principles Established
states.description: The principles, constraints, and baseline industry alignments are established.

states.name: Foundation Established
states.description: The key practices, workflow models, and logical definitions are selected.

states.name: In Use
states.description: Team members are using behavioral walkthroughs to adapt to the way-of-working.

states.name: In Place
states.description: The practices are fully integrated into daily activities.

states.name: Working Well
states.description: The way of working is highly efficient, automated, and demonstrably successful.

states.name: Retired
states.description: The way of working is no longer needed.

alphas.name: Platform Governance
alphas.description: Automated controls, policies, and guardrails

states.name: Scoped
states.description: The need for governance is recognized.

states.name: Documented
states.description: Initial policies are defined.

states.name: Audited
states.description: Policies are actively applied.

alphas.name: Platform Risk And Compliance
alphas.description: Measures the business risk evaluation, security posture validation, and compliance mitigation maturity.

states.name: Identified
states.description: Basic security risks and compliance needs are listed.

states.name: Assessed
states.description: Detailed risk assessment matrices and compliance mappings are documented.

states.name: Mitigated
states.description: Scenario-based behavioral guides mitigate specific user risks.

states.name: Automated
states.description: Automated compliance auditing and security posture checks are in place.

alphas.name: Organizational Change
alphas.description: The organizational patterns, business rationale, and change management required to support the platform transformation.

states.name: Recognized
states.description: Rationale for change is identified.

states.name: Strategized
states.description: Change plans and communication pathways are mapped.

states.name: Enabled
states.description: Playbooks addressing behavioral pushback are executed.

states.name: Embedded
states.description: Comprehensive change management toolkits and automated feedback surveys are deployed.

activitySpaces.name: Explore Possibilities
activitySpaces.description: Explore the possibilities presented by the creation of a new or improved platform.

activitySpaces.name: Assess Business Value
activitySpaces.description: Conduct rigorous business analysis to quantify potential ROI, map platform capabilities to organizational value streams, and secure executive sponsorship.

activitySpaces.name: Monitor Value Realization
activitySpaces.description: Track KPIs such as deployment frequency, MTTR, and developer adoption rates to proactively manage bottlenecks and prove continuous ROI.

activitySpaces.name: Manage Platform Economics
activitySpaces.description: Define chargeback/showback models, right-size infrastructure, optimize costs through FinOps practices, and transition from CapEx to OpEx.

activitySpaces.name: Engage Platform Consumers
activitySpaces.description: Conduct user research, utilize Jobs-to-be-Done frameworks, and ensure the platform demonstrates value through product management practices.

activitySpaces.name: Evangelize and Support
activitySpaces.description: Provide internal marketing, create feedback loops, and deliver accessible support to ensure continuous voluntary adoption by stream-aligned teams.

activitySpaces.name: Establish Secure Guardrails
activitySpaces.description: Shift security left, embed Zero Trust principles, and codify compliance requirements into automated scanning tools to ensure secure-by-default platform operations.

activitySpaces.name: Define Platform Capabilities
activitySpaces.description: Distill stakeholder feedback into actionable requirements and define the Thinnest Viable Platform (TVP) to avoid over-engineering.

activitySpaces.name: Architect and Build the Foundation
activitySpaces.description: Establish declarative provisioning (IaC), build CI/CD pipelines, configure connectivity, deploy orchestration engines, and instantiate the six pillars of platform engineering.

activitySpaces.name: Operate and Evolve the System
activitySpaces.description: Execute Day-2 operations using SRE practices, manage observability telemetry, ensure high availability, and continuously evolve the platform.

activitySpaces.name: Develop the Golden Paths
activitySpaces.description: Build Internal Developer Portals (IDPs), intuitive CLIs, and automated scaffolding templates to drastically reduce cognitive load and enable autonomous self-service.

activitySpaces.name: Integrate Toolchain Services
activitySpaces.description: Specify, acquire, and securely integrate individual platform assets ensuring seamless interoperability with established Golden Paths.

activitySpaces.name: Prepare To Do The Work
activitySpaces.description: Prepare to do the work required for the platform.

activitySpaces.name: Coordinate Delivery Sprints
activitySpaces.description: Manage agile delivery cycles, allocate engineering capacity, and track velocity to ensure predictable platform feature development.

activitySpaces.name: Structure Organizational Topologies
activitySpaces.description: Define clear team interaction modes, establish X-as-a-Service boundaries, and continuously assess cognitive load using Team Topologies principles.

activitySpaces.name: Establish Operational Practices
activitySpaces.description: Define incident response procedures, institute blameless post-mortems, standardize CI methodologies, and foster a continuous-learning culture.

activitySpaces.name: Implement Policy-as-Code
activitySpaces.description: Translate manual governance rules into automated, machine-readable policies that execute within deployment pipelines without impeding velocity.

activitySpaces.name: Drive Cultural Transformation
activitySpaces.description: Execute formal change management programs, upskill engineering talent, address behavioral resistance, and facilitate the shift to product-driven platform engineering.

activitySpaces.name: Stop The Work
activitySpaces.description: Stop the work and close out the endeavor.

narrativeTypes.name: The STAR Format
narrativeTypes.description: Enforces a strict cause-and-effect relationship between context and outcomes (Situation, Task, Action, Result).

narrativeElements.name: Situation
narrativeElements.description: The context or background of the challenge.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the specific situation, context, or baseline state before action is taken.

narrativeElements.name: Task
narrativeElements.description: The specific challenge, objective, or requirement.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Outline the specific task, problem, or goal that needs to be addressed.

narrativeElements.name: Action
narrativeElements.description: The specific steps or interventions performed.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the methodology, activities, or steps taken to address the task.

narrativeElements.name: Result
narrativeElements.description: The outcome, impact, or value achieved.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Summarize the measurable results, outcomes, or state changes achieved from the actions.

narrativeTypes.name: The Hero's Journey
narrativeTypes.description: Highly effective for macro-level lifecycle orchestrations (platform adoptions, transformations).

narrativeElements.name: The Ordinary World
narrativeElements.description: The starting point before the transformation.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the current, pre-platform state of the organization.

narrativeElements.name: The Call to Adventure
narrativeElements.description: The catalyst for change.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Outline the business opportunity, crisis, or driver that necessitates the platform transformation.

narrativeElements.name: The Ordeal
narrativeElements.description: The core transformation challenges and execution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the complex adoption activities, migrations, and challenges faced during implementation.

narrativeElements.name: The Return
narrativeElements.description: The new operational baseline and realized value.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the successful adoption, the accrual of benefits, and the new optimized way of working.

narrativeTypes.name: The Three-Act Structure & StoryBrand
narrativeTypes.description: Positions the consumer as the Hero and the Platform Engineering team as the Guide utilizing the defined approach.

narrativeElements.name: Act I: The Hero and the Problem
narrativeElements.description: Identifying the consumer and their pain points.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Identify the primary consumer (the Hero) and detail the specific friction or problem they face.

narrativeElements.name: Act II: The Guide and the Plan
narrativeElements.description: The platform team offers a solution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Introduce the Platform Engineering team as the Guide who provides a clear, paved-path approach or plan.

narrativeElements.name: Act III: Call to Action and Success
narrativeElements.description: Execution and outcome.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the call to action for the consumer to adopt the plan, and the successful outcome of doing so.

narrativeTypes.name: Micro-Narratives (ABT)
narrativeTypes.description: Shorter frameworks (And/But/Therefore) designed for rapid, highly persuasive daily execution updates.

narrativeElements.name: And (Context)
narrativeElements.description: The current situation and baseline facts.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State the current agreed-upon context, background, and baseline facts.

narrativeElements.name: But (Conflict)
narrativeElements.description: The problem, challenge, or contradiction.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Introduce the specific problem, blocker, challenge, or contradiction encountered.

narrativeElements.name: Therefore (Resolution)
narrativeElements.description: The action taken or conclusion reached.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State the specific action taken, decision made, or conclusion reached to resolve the conflict.

narrativeTypes.name: User story
narrativeTypes.description: A brief, informal explanation of a software feature written from the perspective of the end user.

narrativeElements.name: As a [role]
narrativeElements.description: This identifies the specific persona or role interacting with the feature. It avoids the generic term **the user** to provide context on their technical ability, permissions, and needs.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to define constraints. Instead of saying "user," say "First-time Visitor" or "System Administrator." This helps the developers understand if the UI should be "idiot-proof" or "power-user focused."

narrativeElements.name: I wan to [perform some action]
narrativeElements.description: This is the intent or the feature itself. It describes the action the user wants to take within the software.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Keep this focused on the **what,** not the **how.** Avoid mentioning specific UI elements like **click a red button.** Focus on the functional capability you are giving them.

narrativeElements.name: So that [I can achieve some goal]
narrativeElements.description: This is the purpose. It explains the underlying problem the user is trying to solve or the value they hope to gain.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to justify the work. If you can’t find a compelling **So that** statement, the feature might not be worth building. It also helps developers suggest better technical solutions if they understand the ultimate goal.

narrativeTypes.name: Epic
narrativeTypes.description: A well-structured Epic provides a "north star" for the team, ensuring everyone knows why a large project exists and what success looks like.

narrativeElements.name: Summary
narrativeElements.description: A clear, punchy title and a one-sentence elevator pitch that describes the high-level initiative.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Treat this as the project's identity. Use it in stakeholder meetings and roadmap views to provide an instant understanding of what is being built without getting bogged down in details.

narrativeElements.name: Strategic Intent
narrativeElements.description: This section explains how this Epic aligns with the company's broader business goals or quarterly objectives (OKRs).
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to justify the budget and resource allocation. If you can't link the Epic back to a specific business value (e.g., "Increasing retention by 10%"), it shouldn't be an Epic.

narrativeElements.name: User Personas
narrativeElements.description: A list of the primary and secondary users who will be impacted by this large-scale change.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to keep the scope focused. When brainstorming features, ask: "Does this specific feature serve the personas listed in the Epic?" If not, it belongs in a different Epic.

narrativeElements.name: High-Level Requirements
narrativeElements.description: These are not detailed stories yet, but rather the broad capabilities the system must have once the Epic is finished.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use these as "themes" to help you brainstorm the individual User Stories later. They serve as the framework for your backlog.

narrativeElements.name: Success Metrics
narrativeElements.description: The quantitative data points that will prove the Epic was a success after it is released.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to define the "Definition of Done" for the entire project. Instead of saying "when the code is finished," use "when the checkout conversion rate hits 5%."

narrativeTypes.name: Lifecycle
narrativeTypes.description: A standard lifecycle orchestration framework to map progression phases.

narrativeElements.name: Prerequisites
narrativeElements.description: Conditions required before starting the lifecycle.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Define the Phase 0 or preparation steps, including baseline checks or prerequisite states, that must be achieved before the main lifecycle begins.

narrativeElements.name: Lifecycle Phase
narrativeElements.description: An active stage of lifecycle execution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the active state transitions, required work products, and activities for this specific phase of the lifecycle progression.

narrativeTypes.name: Essay Narrative
narrativeTypes.description: A cohesive narrative format that guides the reader carefully through the evidence for and against a proposition before reaching a conclusion.

narrativeElements.name: Introduction
narrativeElements.description: The start of the essay used to contextualise the work and grab the attention of the reader.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Explain how the topic sits within the framework of the subject area as a whole. Outline the structure of your essay very briefly, but do not give your conclusions away on the first page.

narrativeElements.name: Defining Key Concepts
narrativeElements.description: A section establishing the interpretation of central concepts without relying on dictionary definitions.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Relate in your own words how the terms you will be using are to be interpreted within the context of your essay.

narrativeElements.name: Presenting Evidence
narrativeElements.description: The core discussion where secondary works are evaluated and viewpoints are balanced against each other.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Be selective in your choice of evidence and use signposting language to guide your reader. Quote sparingly, paraphrase occasionally, and summarise often to integrate other people's ideas into your own argument.

narrativeElements.name: Conclusion
narrativeElements.description: The closing section that synthesises the presented evidence and forms a direct response to the assignment title.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Draw the threads of your argument together. Do not bring in new evidence in your concluding paragraphs or try to cram in ideas that you have not developed fully.

narrativeTypes.name: Report Narrative
narrativeTypes.description: A formal, informative structure broken down into sections and sub-sections to order and communicate relevant information in an easily navigable way.

narrativeElements.name: Executive Summary
narrativeElements.description: A stand-alone summary of the entire report's purpose, methodology, findings, conclusions, and recommendations.
narrativeElements.howToUse: This should be the last thing that you write. Keep it concise (usually a paragraph or two and always less than a page) to enable the reader to make an informed decision about whether they want to read the report itself.

narrativeElements.name: Introduction
narrativeElements.description: Explains the rationale for undertaking the work reported on, the background, and the scope of the report.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State what the report is about, define how it meets the requirements of the brief, and explain your research methods.

narrativeElements.name: Methods
narrativeElements.description: A clear description of how the investigation was carried out and why specific methods were chosen.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Write this section concisely but thoroughly. Provide step-by-step details in such a way that a reader could replicate the research you have done.

narrativeElements.name: Results and Findings
narrativeElements.description: A purely factual presentation of the research data using text, graphs, tables, or diagrams.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Present the findings of your research as simply as possible. Save your interpretation of the results for the Discussion section.

narrativeElements.name: Discussion
narrativeElements.description: The section that brings everything together by showing how the findings relate to the purpose of the report and previous research.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Interpret the results, showing how they respond to the brief explained in the introduction. Mention if there were any problems or unexpected results and how they were solved.

narrativeElements.name: Recommendations
narrativeElements.description: Suggestions for a future course of action based on the evidence and conclusions.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Make recommendations that solve problems or help to develop a new strategy. Make an effort to sound authoritative and certain in your choices.

narrativeTypes.name: Citation Standard
narrativeTypes.description: The structural elements required for a reference list entry.

narrativeElements.name: Author
narrativeElements.description: The person, group, or organization responsible for the work.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Invert authors' names (Lastname, F. M.). Use an ampersand (&) before the final author's name in a list. For groups, use the full name.

narrativeElements.name: Date
narrativeElements.description: The publication date of the work.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Enclose the year in parentheses, followed by a period: (2026). For works with no date, use (n.d.).

narrativeElements.name: Title
narrativeElements.description: The name of the specific work being cited.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Italicize the title of standalone works (books, reports). Use sentence case—capitalize only the first word of the title and subtitle.

narrativeElements.name: Source
narrativeElements.description: Where the work can be retrieved, such as a journal, publisher, or URL.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Include the periodical title and volume/issue if applicable. Provide a DOI or URL as a live link; do not include 'Retrieved from' for most entries.

narrativeTypes.name: The STAR Format
narrativeTypes.description: Enforces a strict cause-and-effect relationship between context and outcomes (Situation, Task, Action, Result).

narrativeElements.name: Situation
narrativeElements.description: The context or background of the challenge.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the specific situation, context, or baseline state before action is taken.

narrativeElements.name: Task
narrativeElements.description: The specific challenge, objective, or requirement.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Outline the specific task, problem, or goal that needs to be addressed.

narrativeElements.name: Action
narrativeElements.description: The specific steps or interventions performed.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the methodology, activities, or steps taken to address the task.

narrativeElements.name: Result
narrativeElements.description: The outcome, impact, or value achieved.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Summarize the measurable results, outcomes, or state changes achieved from the actions.

narrativeTypes.name: The Hero's Journey
narrativeTypes.description: Highly effective for macro-level lifecycle orchestrations (platform adoptions, transformations).

narrativeElements.name: The Ordinary World
narrativeElements.description: The starting point before the transformation.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the current, pre-platform state of the organization.

narrativeElements.name: The Call to Adventure
narrativeElements.description: The catalyst for change.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Outline the business opportunity, crisis, or driver that necessitates the platform transformation.

narrativeElements.name: The Ordeal
narrativeElements.description: The core transformation challenges and execution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the complex adoption activities, migrations, and challenges faced during implementation.

narrativeElements.name: The Return
narrativeElements.description: The new operational baseline and realized value.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the successful adoption, the accrual of benefits, and the new optimized way of working.

narrativeTypes.name: The Three-Act Structure & StoryBrand
narrativeTypes.description: Positions the consumer as the Hero and the Platform Engineering team as the Guide utilizing the defined approach.

narrativeElements.name: Act I: The Hero and the Problem
narrativeElements.description: Identifying the consumer and their pain points.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Identify the primary consumer (the Hero) and detail the specific friction or problem they face.

narrativeElements.name: Act II: The Guide and the Plan
narrativeElements.description: The platform team offers a solution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Introduce the Platform Engineering team as the Guide who provides a clear, paved-path approach or plan.

narrativeElements.name: Act III: Call to Action and Success
narrativeElements.description: Execution and outcome.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the call to action for the consumer to adopt the plan, and the successful outcome of doing so.

narrativeTypes.name: Micro-Narratives (ABT)
narrativeTypes.description: Shorter frameworks (And/But/Therefore) designed for rapid, highly persuasive daily execution updates.

narrativeElements.name: And (Context)
narrativeElements.description: The current situation and baseline facts.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State the current agreed-upon context, background, and baseline facts.

narrativeElements.name: But (Conflict)
narrativeElements.description: The problem, challenge, or contradiction.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Introduce the specific problem, blocker, challenge, or contradiction encountered.

narrativeElements.name: Therefore (Resolution)
narrativeElements.description: The action taken or conclusion reached.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State the specific action taken, decision made, or conclusion reached to resolve the conflict.

narrativeTypes.name: User story
narrativeTypes.description: A brief, informal explanation of a software feature written from the perspective of the end user.

narrativeElements.name: As a [role]
narrativeElements.description: This identifies the specific persona or role interacting with the feature. It avoids the generic term **the user** to provide context on their technical ability, permissions, and needs.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to define constraints. Instead of saying "user," say "First-time Visitor" or "System Administrator." This helps the developers understand if the UI should be "idiot-proof" or "power-user focused."

narrativeElements.name: I wan to [perform some action]
narrativeElements.description: This is the intent or the feature itself. It describes the action the user wants to take within the software.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Keep this focused on the **what,** not the **how.** Avoid mentioning specific UI elements like **click a red button.** Focus on the functional capability you are giving them.

narrativeElements.name: So that [I can achieve some goal]
narrativeElements.description: This is the purpose. It explains the underlying problem the user is trying to solve or the value they hope to gain.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to justify the work. If you can’t find a compelling **So that** statement, the feature might not be worth building. It also helps developers suggest better technical solutions if they understand the ultimate goal.

narrativeTypes.name: Epic
narrativeTypes.description: A well-structured Epic provides a "north star" for the team, ensuring everyone knows why a large project exists and what success looks like.

narrativeElements.name: Summary
narrativeElements.description: A clear, punchy title and a one-sentence elevator pitch that describes the high-level initiative.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Treat this as the project's identity. Use it in stakeholder meetings and roadmap views to provide an instant understanding of what is being built without getting bogged down in details.

narrativeElements.name: Strategic Intent
narrativeElements.description: This section explains how this Epic aligns with the company's broader business goals or quarterly objectives (OKRs).
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to justify the budget and resource allocation. If you can't link the Epic back to a specific business value (e.g., "Increasing retention by 10%"), it shouldn't be an Epic.

narrativeElements.name: User Personas
narrativeElements.description: A list of the primary and secondary users who will be impacted by this large-scale change.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to keep the scope focused. When brainstorming features, ask: "Does this specific feature serve the personas listed in the Epic?" If not, it belongs in a different Epic.

narrativeElements.name: High-Level Requirements
narrativeElements.description: These are not detailed stories yet, but rather the broad capabilities the system must have once the Epic is finished.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use these as "themes" to help you brainstorm the individual User Stories later. They serve as the framework for your backlog.

narrativeElements.name: Success Metrics
narrativeElements.description: The quantitative data points that will prove the Epic was a success after it is released.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to define the "Definition of Done" for the entire project. Instead of saying "when the code is finished," use "when the checkout conversion rate hits 5%."

narrativeTypes.name: Lifecycle
narrativeTypes.description: A standard lifecycle orchestration framework to map progression phases.

narrativeElements.name: Prerequisites
narrativeElements.description: Conditions required before starting the lifecycle.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Define the Phase 0 or preparation steps, including baseline checks or prerequisite states, that must be achieved before the main lifecycle begins.

narrativeElements.name: Lifecycle Phase
narrativeElements.description: An active stage of lifecycle execution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the active state transitions, required work products, and activities for this specific phase of the lifecycle progression.

narrativeTypes.name: Essay Narrative
narrativeTypes.description: A cohesive narrative format that guides the reader carefully through the evidence for and against a proposition before reaching a conclusion.

narrativeElements.name: Introduction
narrativeElements.description: The start of the essay used to contextualise the work and grab the attention of the reader.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Explain how the topic sits within the framework of the subject area as a whole. Outline the structure of your essay very briefly, but do not give your conclusions away on the first page.

narrativeElements.name: Defining Key Concepts
narrativeElements.description: A section establishing the interpretation of central concepts without relying on dictionary definitions.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Relate in your own words how the terms you will be using are to be interpreted within the context of your essay.

narrativeElements.name: Presenting Evidence
narrativeElements.description: The core discussion where secondary works are evaluated and viewpoints are balanced against each other.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Be selective in your choice of evidence and use signposting language to guide your reader. Quote sparingly, paraphrase occasionally, and summarise often to integrate other people's ideas into your own argument.

narrativeElements.name: Conclusion
narrativeElements.description: The closing section that synthesises the presented evidence and forms a direct response to the assignment title.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Draw the threads of your argument together. Do not bring in new evidence in your concluding paragraphs or try to cram in ideas that you have not developed fully.

narrativeTypes.name: Report Narrative
narrativeTypes.description: A formal, informative structure broken down into sections and sub-sections to order and communicate relevant information in an easily navigable way.

narrativeElements.name: Executive Summary
narrativeElements.description: A stand-alone summary of the entire report's purpose, methodology, findings, conclusions, and recommendations.
narrativeElements.howToUse: This should be the last thing that you write. Keep it concise (usually a paragraph or two and always less than a page) to enable the reader to make an informed decision about whether they want to read the report itself.

narrativeElements.name: Introduction
narrativeElements.description: Explains the rationale for undertaking the work reported on, the background, and the scope of the report.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State what the report is about, define how it meets the requirements of the brief, and explain your research methods.

narrativeElements.name: Methods
narrativeElements.description: A clear description of how the investigation was carried out and why specific methods were chosen.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Write this section concisely but thoroughly. Provide step-by-step details in such a way that a reader could replicate the research you have done.

narrativeElements.name: Results and Findings
narrativeElements.description: A purely factual presentation of the research data using text, graphs, tables, or diagrams.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Present the findings of your research as simply as possible. Save your interpretation of the results for the Discussion section.

narrativeElements.name: Discussion
narrativeElements.description: The section that brings everything together by showing how the findings relate to the purpose of the report and previous research.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Interpret the results, showing how they respond to the brief explained in the introduction. Mention if there were any problems or unexpected results and how they were solved.

narrativeElements.name: Recommendations
narrativeElements.description: Suggestions for a future course of action based on the evidence and conclusions.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Make recommendations that solve problems or help to develop a new strategy. Make an effort to sound authoritative and certain in your choices.

narrativeTypes.name: Citation Standard
narrativeTypes.description: The structural elements required for a reference list entry.

narrativeElements.name: Author
narrativeElements.description: The person, group, or organization responsible for the work.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Invert authors' names (Lastname, F. M.). Use an ampersand (&) before the final author's name in a list. For groups, use the full name.

narrativeElements.name: Date
narrativeElements.description: The publication date of the work.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Enclose the year in parentheses, followed by a period: (2026). For works with no date, use (n.d.).

narrativeElements.name: Title
narrativeElements.description: The name of the specific work being cited.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Italicize the title of standalone works (books, reports). Use sentence case—capitalize only the first word of the title and subtitle.

narrativeElements.name: Source
narrativeElements.description: Where the work can be retrieved, such as a journal, publisher, or URL.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Include the periodical title and volume/issue if applicable. Provide a DOI or URL as a live link; do not include 'Retrieved from' for most entries.

practices.name: OpenShift Cluster Foundation
practices.description: This practice defines the foundational activities, artifacts, and roles required to establish a stable OpenShift 4.21 cluster. It focuses on the transition from high-level architectural requirements to a baselined platform state where the control plane and node infrastructure are operational.

narratives.name: Practice Overview
narratives.description: Overview of the Cluster Foundation practice.

narrativeContexts.context: The foundation practice addresses the critical need for a resilient control plane, which acts as the 'brain' of the OpenShift environment.
It prioritizes the use of Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (RHCOS) and Ignition for immutable, automated node provisioning, which requires a shift from manual configurations.
Establishing this foundation allows organizations to confidently support diverse workloads, from core datacenters to resource-constrained edge devices.

alphas.name: Platform
alphas.description: The unified system of assets and interfaces provided to consumers.

narratives.name: Platform Architecture Details
narratives.description: Details about OpenShift modular architecture.

narrativeContexts.context: The essential container orchestration environment includes the control plane and the machine-managed node infrastructure.
OpenShift 4.21 uses a modular architecture where cluster functions are managed by internal Operators, each responsible for its own lifecycle and state.
The control plane hosts critical components like etcd, which stores the environment’s state and requires high availability for cluster stability.

states.description: The foundational structure is chosen.

checklist.description: The YAML file contains the valid pull secret, base domain, and SSH keys.

checklist.description: All three master nodes have joined the etcd cluster and are in a 'Running' state.

checklist.name: Cluster Operators Available
checklist.description: The oc get clusteroperators command shows all operators as available and non-degraded.

states.name: Ready
states.description: The platform is fully operational.

checklist.name: Console Accessible
checklist.description: The web-based management UI is reachable via the defined ingress route.

checklist.name: Authentication Configured
checklist.description: The initial kubeadmin user can log in, or a preliminary identity provider is configured.

checklist.name: DNS Resolution Verified

checklist.name: Post-install Config Applied
checklist.description: Standard configurations (NTP, registry mirroring, custom certificates) are documented and applied.

workProducts.name: Installation Configuration
workProducts.description: The primary artifact (install-config.yaml) used by the OpenShift installer to define the cluster's infrastructure.

narratives.name: Install Config Summary
narratives.description: Defines the core installation inputs.

narrativeContexts.context: The install configuration provides the core parameters for infrastructure definition.
It must be precisely formatted to include pull secrets and domains without error.
Validating this artifact ensures stable downstream Ignition generation.

levelsOfDetail.name: Outlined
levelsOfDetail.description: A basic template containing cluster name, base domain, and SSH keys.

checklist.name: Cluster Name Defined
checklist.description: Unique identifier for the OCP deployment is set.

checklist.name: Base Domain Present
checklist.description: The parent DNS domain is specified for the cluster endpoints.

checklist.name: Pull Secret Included
checklist.description: Valid Red Hat pull secret is embedded for image access.

levelsOfDetail.name: Detailed
levelsOfDetail.description: A comprehensive configuration including cloud provider specifics, machine pools, and proxy settings.

checklist.name: Machine Pools Configured
checklist.description: Replicas and instance types for control plane and compute nodes are defined.

checklist.name: Network Type Specified
checklist.description: CNI selection (OVN-Kubernetes or OpenShiftSDN) is documented.

checklist.name: Platform Parameters Validated
checklist.description: Cloud-specific settings (VPC IDs, Subnets, Resource Groups) are verified.

workProducts.name: Ignition Configuration
workProducts.description: Machine-specific JSON files generated from the installer that automate the first boot of RHCOS nodes.

narratives.name: Ignition Summary
narratives.description: Explains how Ignition files operate.

narrativeContexts.context: Ignition files replace manual scripting for OS configuration.
They must be generated securely and distributed to nodes during the PXE or cloud init phase.
Providing automated JSON manifests ensures every node boots uniformly.

levelsOfDetail.name: Defined
levelsOfDetail.description: Logical set of bootstrap, master, and worker ignition files.

checklist.name: File System Layout Ready
checklist.description: Partitioning and formatting instructions are included.

checklist.name: Systemd Units Configured
checklist.description: Essential services for cluster startup are defined in the JSON.

levelsOfDetail.name: Automated
levelsOfDetail.description: Production-ready Ignition files served via HTTP or integrated into cloud user data.

checklist.name: SSH Keys Injected
checklist.description: Secure access is established for initial node troubleshooting.

checklist.name: Certificate Authority Embedded
checklist.description: Cluster-wide CAs are present for secure communication.

personas.name: Platform Architect
personas.description: Responsible for high-level infrastructure design, selecting hosting platforms, and ensuring the architecture meets availability requirements.

narratives.name: Architect Role Context
narratives.description: Focuses on high level design.

narrativeContexts.context: The Platform Architect designs the broad topology.
They must balance cloud requirements with on-premise constraints.
Their output ensures infrastructural soundness before provisioning begins.

personas.name: Cluster Administrator
personas.description: Handles the technical installation, node management, and Day 1 configuration tasks.

narratives.name: Admin Role Context
narratives.description: Executes the deployment.

narrativeContexts.context: The Cluster Admin manages the day to day node tasks.
Installation parameters require strict attention to YAML validity.
They execute the installer and validate the core operators.

personaGroups.name: Platform Core Team
personaGroups.description: The centralized group responsible for the establishment and stability of the OpenShift foundation.

narratives.name: Core Team Dynamic
narratives.description: How the team collaborates.

narrativeContexts.context: The core team brings together strategy and execution.
Both aspects are necessary to prevent architectural drift.
They form a cohesive group driving the initial lifecycle.

activities.name: Infrastructure Design
activities.description: Defining the hardware or cloud resources, networking topology, and capacity requirements for the cluster.

narratives.name: Design Context
narratives.description: Activity detail.

narrativeContexts.context: Design must be finalized before execution.
Capacity requirements change based on workloads.

practices.name: OpenShift Pilot Infrastructure Delivery
practices.description: This practice defines the strict technical execution required to establish the foundational compute, network, and storage topology for the OpenShift Container Platform Pilot. It extends baseline cluster foundation principles to orchestrate the sequential deployment of three distinct environments: Sandbox, Non-Production, and Production. The practice dictates a paradigm shift toward immutable infrastructure management, relying heavily on GitOps workflows, Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (RHCOS), and automated Ignition configurations to ensure repeatable, scalable, and secure cluster provisioning across hybrid ecosystems.

narratives.name: Infrastructure Immutability Strategy
narratives.description: The necessity of moving away from manual node configuration toward automated, declarative GitOps models.

narrativeContexts.context: Traditional virtualization administrators and IT operations teams often rely on the manual, stateful configuration of underlying host systems. This legacy approach inevitably leads to severe configuration drift, undetected security vulnerabilities, and highly brittle disaster recovery processes that cannot scale in a cloud-native environment.

The OpenShift Pilot infrastructure delivery model strictly prohibits this legacy imperative approach. Instead, it mandates the absolute use of immutable infrastructure via Red Hat Enterprise Linux CoreOS (RHCOS) and machine-specific JSON Ignition files, which are generated systematically from declarative YAML manifests.

Furthermore, ongoing cluster operations, role-based access controls, and state management are governed entirely by Declarative GitOps Configurations. This ensures that the entire platform state is continuously version-controlled, fully auditable, and capable of instantaneous, automated drift reconciliation.

This architectural pivot not only accelerates the reliable provisioning of the required Sandbox, Non-Production, and Production clusters, but it also establishes an inherently resilient foundation capable of supporting highly advanced enterprise integrations, such as OpenShift AI, large-scale data science workloads, and dynamic Tanzu Application Platforms.

narratives.name: Cluster Progression

narrativeContexts.context: Operating a single, isolated cluster is wholly insufficient to validate the operational readiness, security posture, and lifecycle management capabilities of an enterprise-grade platform. Delivery teams must establish a progressive chain of distinct environments to safely isolate experimental testing from mission-critical live workloads.

The Sandbox cluster acts as the fundamental reference installation, proving the underlying infrastructure integration and network ingress. Subsequently, the Non-Production cluster serves as the dedicated proving ground for developers, while the Production cluster is hardened exclusively for end-users, requiring strictly enforced sizing, security policies, and integration profiles.

narratives.name: The End of Manual Drift

narrativeContexts.context: Managing complex, highly distributed systems via manual command-line interface interventions is a common legacy practice.
This approach introduces unacceptable, systemic risks regarding configuration drift, human error, and compliance violations.

The GitOps Governance alpha ensures that all cluster state changes are fully auditable, subject to rigorous peer review via pull requests, and automatically reconciled by in-cluster software operators, preventing unauthorized alterations.

practices.name: Application Onboarding & Release Engineering
practices.description: This practice operationalizes the delivery of true business value by systematically transitioning applications from legacy, monolithic deployments into the modern OpenShift environment. It encompasses the meticulous containerization of target workloads, the engineering of robust, highly repeatable CI/CD deployment pipelines, and the implementation of software delivery metrics dashboards (such as Pelorus) to accurately quantify adoption success, deployment frequency, and lead time for code changes. This practice ensures that developers can consume the platform efficiently without compromising security or operational stability.

narratives.name: The Value Realization Engine
narratives.description: An explanation of why establishing infrastructure alone is entirely insufficient without successful application onboarding.

narrativeContexts.context: An exquisitely provisioned, highly available Kubernetes cluster holds zero inherent business value until applications are actively serving end-user traffic.
Moving stateful legacy apps onto containers manually defeats the purpose of the platform.

This practice bridges the critical gap between raw infrastructure availability and actual developer productivity. By enforcing the use of parameterized, environment-agnostic Kubernetes resources and fully automated continuous integration pipelines, organizations shift permanently away from manual, error-prone release management. This accelerates time-to-market, drastically reduces deployment failures, and ultimately enhances overall system resilience. Furthermore, the explicit requirement to implement metrics dashboards ensures that executive stakeholders can transparently validate the return on investment through empirical data detailing improved software delivery performance.

practices.name: Container Platform Pilot Lifecycle Orchestration
practices.description: This practice serves as the critical macro-level governance and project management layer. It organizes the entire engagement through the Services Delivery Framework and the Mobius Loop. It meticulously manages scoping complexity (differentiating single from multiple products), calculates capacity task estimates, maintains cross-functional team alignment, and oversees the production of the Consulting Engagement Report (CER). It ensures that deep technical delivery across both infrastructure and application workstreams remains strictly tethered to the customer's strategic business outcomes.

narratives.name: Governing the Journey
narratives.description: Applying the Mobius Loop and strict phase-gating to control engagement complexity and mitigate implementation risks.

narrativeContexts.context: Without rigorous project management and formalized strategic oversight, highly technical infrastructure builds and complex application containerization tasks frequently succumb to dangerous scope creep and severely misaligned stakeholder expectations.
Technical delivery without a framework leads to failure.

This practice forcefully enforces the Mobius Loop lifecycle—progressing systematically through Discovery, Options, Delivery, and Foundation. It ensures that the critical 'Delivery' phase is broken down into three distinct, highly monitored milestones (Sandbox, Non-Prod, Prod) that require the satisfaction of specific entrance and exit criteria before progression is permitted. Furthermore, the orchestration practice calculates the Project Complexity Matrix. It distributes manual hours, defines precise staffing models, and mitigates risks to guarantee an optimized percent chance of successful project closure while remaining compliant with legal contracting requirements.

narratives.name: Strategic Transformation and Mind-Shift
narratives.description: The strategic transition from siloed legacy tools to a unified platform ecosystem.

narrativeContexts.context: Enterprise IT managers face hurdles such as operational complexity and security risks when managing siloed tools across multiple cloud providers. Adopting OpenShift Virtualization requires a significant mental shift for teams familiar with traditional virtualization tooling.

Organizations must achieve faster releases, improved service delivery, and optimized costs through granular resource allocation while structurally integrating Infrastructure-as-a-Service (IaaS) and Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) teams into a single collaborative unit.

By moving through the OEAM, the organization standardizes workloads, boosting efficiency through CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure-as-code, and automated provisioning, supported by close involvement from technical experts.
The learning curve is mitigated, resulting in a unified platform that reduces operational complexity, standardizes cross-cloud environments, and provides scalable architectural readiness.

narratives.name: Strategic Intent and Methodological Value
narratives.narrativeName: Driving Enterprise Transformation through Sustainable Flow
narratives.description: The overarching strategy and value proposition of the OpenShift Pilot delivery methodology.

narrativeContexts.context: Enterprise organizations consistently struggle to modernize application delivery due to fragmented legacy infrastructure, siloed operational teams, and a lack of standardized, repeatable deployment workflows. This method addresses these systemic bottlenecks by implementing a standardized consulting delivery framework that mandates declarative automation and immutable infrastructure patterns across all environments.

The fundamental execution strategy relies heavily on the Mobius Loop, an infinity-loop framework that drives continuous, sustainable flow through four distinct phases: Discovery, Options, Delivery, and Foundation. This structural approach ensures that deep technical implementation tasks remain perpetually aligned with measurable, strategic business value.

By explicitly defining scoping outcomes, dynamic project complexity matrices, and highly robust capacity planning models—including the calculation of maximum hours per week per specialized role—the method dramatically mitigates engagement risks. It ensures that executive sponsors, infrastructure engineers, and application developers are fully synchronized throughout the transformation journey.

Ultimately, the successful execution of this unified method yields a minimally viable operational capability for the enterprise. This capability is evidenced by the successful deployment of three distinct cluster environments, fully automated software delivery pipelines, and comprehensive Consulting Engagement Reports (CER) that provide a definitive, validated roadmap for future organizational scaling.

narrativeTypes.name: The STAR Format
narrativeTypes.description: Enforces a strict cause-and-effect relationship between context and outcomes (Situation, Task, Action, Result).

narrativeElements.name: Situation
narrativeElements.description: The context or background of the challenge.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the specific situation, context, or baseline state before action is taken.

narrativeElements.name: Task
narrativeElements.description: The specific challenge, objective, or requirement.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Outline the specific task, problem, or goal that needs to be addressed.

narrativeElements.name: Action
narrativeElements.description: The specific steps or interventions performed.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the methodology, activities, or steps taken to address the task.

narrativeElements.name: Result
narrativeElements.description: The outcome, impact, or value achieved.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Summarize the measurable results, outcomes, or state changes achieved from the actions.

narrativeTypes.name: The Hero's Journey
narrativeTypes.description: Highly effective for macro-level lifecycle orchestrations (platform adoptions, transformations).

narrativeElements.name: The Ordinary World
narrativeElements.description: The starting point before the transformation.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the current, pre-platform state of the organization.

narrativeElements.name: The Call to Adventure
narrativeElements.description: The catalyst for change.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Outline the business opportunity, crisis, or driver that necessitates the platform transformation.

narrativeElements.name: The Ordeal
narrativeElements.description: The core transformation challenges and execution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the complex adoption activities, migrations, and challenges faced during implementation.

narrativeElements.name: The Return
narrativeElements.description: The new operational baseline and realized value.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the successful adoption, the accrual of benefits, and the new optimized way of working.

narrativeTypes.name: The Three-Act Structure & StoryBrand
narrativeTypes.description: Positions the consumer as the Hero and the Platform Engineering team as the Guide utilizing the defined approach.

narrativeElements.name: Act I: The Hero and the Problem
narrativeElements.description: Identifying the consumer and their pain points.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Identify the primary consumer (the Hero) and detail the specific friction or problem they face.

narrativeElements.name: Act II: The Guide and the Plan
narrativeElements.description: The platform team offers a solution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Introduce the Platform Engineering team as the Guide who provides a clear, paved-path approach or plan.

narrativeElements.name: Act III: Call to Action and Success
narrativeElements.description: Execution and outcome.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Describe the call to action for the consumer to adopt the plan, and the successful outcome of doing so.

narrativeTypes.name: Micro-Narratives (ABT)
narrativeTypes.description: Shorter frameworks (And/But/Therefore) designed for rapid, highly persuasive daily execution updates.

narrativeElements.name: And (Context)
narrativeElements.description: The current situation and baseline facts.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State the current agreed-upon context, background, and baseline facts.

narrativeElements.name: But (Conflict)
narrativeElements.description: The problem, challenge, or contradiction.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Introduce the specific problem, blocker, challenge, or contradiction encountered.

narrativeElements.name: Therefore (Resolution)
narrativeElements.description: The action taken or conclusion reached.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State the specific action taken, decision made, or conclusion reached to resolve the conflict.

narrativeTypes.name: User story
narrativeTypes.description: A brief, informal explanation of a software feature written from the perspective of the end user.

narrativeElements.name: As a [role]
narrativeElements.description: This identifies the specific persona or role interacting with the feature. It avoids the generic term **the user** to provide context on their technical ability, permissions, and needs.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to define constraints. Instead of saying "user," say "First-time Visitor" or "System Administrator." This helps the developers understand if the UI should be "idiot-proof" or "power-user focused."

narrativeElements.name: I wan to [perform some action]
narrativeElements.description: This is the intent or the feature itself. It describes the action the user wants to take within the software.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Keep this focused on the **what,** not the **how.** Avoid mentioning specific UI elements like **click a red button.** Focus on the functional capability you are giving them.

narrativeElements.name: So that [I can achieve some goal]
narrativeElements.description: This is the purpose. It explains the underlying problem the user is trying to solve or the value they hope to gain.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to justify the work. If you can’t find a compelling **So that** statement, the feature might not be worth building. It also helps developers suggest better technical solutions if they understand the ultimate goal.

narrativeTypes.name: Epic
narrativeTypes.description: A well-structured Epic provides a "north star" for the team, ensuring everyone knows why a large project exists and what success looks like.

narrativeElements.name: Summary
narrativeElements.description: A clear, punchy title and a one-sentence elevator pitch that describes the high-level initiative.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Treat this as the project's identity. Use it in stakeholder meetings and roadmap views to provide an instant understanding of what is being built without getting bogged down in details.

narrativeElements.name: Strategic Intent
narrativeElements.description: This section explains how this Epic aligns with the company's broader business goals or quarterly objectives (OKRs).
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to justify the budget and resource allocation. If you can't link the Epic back to a specific business value (e.g., "Increasing retention by 10%"), it shouldn't be an Epic.

narrativeElements.name: User Personas
narrativeElements.description: A list of the primary and secondary users who will be impacted by this large-scale change.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to keep the scope focused. When brainstorming features, ask: "Does this specific feature serve the personas listed in the Epic?" If not, it belongs in a different Epic.

narrativeElements.name: High-Level Requirements
narrativeElements.description: These are not detailed stories yet, but rather the broad capabilities the system must have once the Epic is finished.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use these as "themes" to help you brainstorm the individual User Stories later. They serve as the framework for your backlog.

narrativeElements.name: Success Metrics
narrativeElements.description: The quantitative data points that will prove the Epic was a success after it is released.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Use this to define the "Definition of Done" for the entire project. Instead of saying "when the code is finished," use "when the checkout conversion rate hits 5%."

narrativeTypes.name: Lifecycle
narrativeTypes.description: A standard lifecycle orchestration framework to map progression phases.

narrativeElements.name: Prerequisites
narrativeElements.description: Conditions required before starting the lifecycle.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Define the Phase 0 or preparation steps, including baseline checks or prerequisite states, that must be achieved before the main lifecycle begins.

narrativeElements.name: Lifecycle Phase
narrativeElements.description: An active stage of lifecycle execution.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Detail the active state transitions, required work products, and activities for this specific phase of the lifecycle progression.

narrativeTypes.name: Essay Narrative
narrativeTypes.description: A cohesive narrative format that guides the reader carefully through the evidence for and against a proposition before reaching a conclusion.

narrativeElements.name: Introduction
narrativeElements.description: The start of the essay used to contextualise the work and grab the attention of the reader.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Explain how the topic sits within the framework of the subject area as a whole. Outline the structure of your essay very briefly, but do not give your conclusions away on the first page.

narrativeElements.name: Defining Key Concepts
narrativeElements.description: A section establishing the interpretation of central concepts without relying on dictionary definitions.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Relate in your own words how the terms you will be using are to be interpreted within the context of your essay.

narrativeElements.name: Presenting Evidence
narrativeElements.description: The core discussion where secondary works are evaluated and viewpoints are balanced against each other.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Be selective in your choice of evidence and use signposting language to guide your reader. Quote sparingly, paraphrase occasionally, and summarise often to integrate other people's ideas into your own argument.

narrativeElements.name: Conclusion
narrativeElements.description: The closing section that synthesises the presented evidence and forms a direct response to the assignment title.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Draw the threads of your argument together. Do not bring in new evidence in your concluding paragraphs or try to cram in ideas that you have not developed fully.

narrativeTypes.name: Report Narrative
narrativeTypes.description: A formal, informative structure broken down into sections and sub-sections to order and communicate relevant information in an easily navigable way.

narrativeElements.name: Executive Summary
narrativeElements.description: A stand-alone summary of the entire report's purpose, methodology, findings, conclusions, and recommendations.
narrativeElements.howToUse: This should be the last thing that you write. Keep it concise (usually a paragraph or two and always less than a page) to enable the reader to make an informed decision about whether they want to read the report itself.

narrativeElements.name: Introduction
narrativeElements.description: Explains the rationale for undertaking the work reported on, the background, and the scope of the report.
narrativeElements.howToUse: State what the report is about, define how it meets the requirements of the brief, and explain your research methods.

narrativeElements.name: Methods
narrativeElements.description: A clear description of how the investigation was carried out and why specific methods were chosen.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Write this section concisely but thoroughly. Provide step-by-step details in such a way that a reader could replicate the research you have done.

narrativeElements.name: Results and Findings
narrativeElements.description: A purely factual presentation of the research data using text, graphs, tables, or diagrams.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Present the findings of your research as simply as possible. Save your interpretation of the results for the Discussion section.

narrativeElements.name: Discussion
narrativeElements.description: The section that brings everything together by showing how the findings relate to the purpose of the report and previous research.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Interpret the results, showing how they respond to the brief explained in the introduction. Mention if there were any problems or unexpected results and how they were solved.

narrativeElements.name: Recommendations
narrativeElements.description: Suggestions for a future course of action based on the evidence and conclusions.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Make recommendations that solve problems or help to develop a new strategy. Make an effort to sound authoritative and certain in your choices.

narrativeTypes.name: Citation Standard
narrativeTypes.description: The structural elements required for a reference list entry.

narrativeElements.name: Author
narrativeElements.description: The person, group, or organization responsible for the work.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Invert authors' names (Lastname, F. M.). Use an ampersand (&) before the final author's name in a list. For groups, use the full name.

narrativeElements.name: Date
narrativeElements.description: The publication date of the work.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Enclose the year in parentheses, followed by a period: (2026). For works with no date, use (n.d.).

narrativeElements.name: Title
narrativeElements.description: The name of the specific work being cited.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Italicize the title of standalone works (books, reports). Use sentence case—capitalize only the first word of the title and subtitle.

narrativeElements.name: Source
narrativeElements.description: Where the work can be retrieved, such as a journal, publisher, or URL.
narrativeElements.howToUse: Include the periodical title and volume/issue if applicable. Provide a DOI or URL as a live link; do not include 'Retrieved from' for most entries.

practices.name: Reliability Practice
practices.description: This practice provides the methodology and structural rigor required to ensure that a cloud workload consistently meets its uptime and recovery targets. It addresses the capacity of a distributed system to anticipate, withstand, and rapidly recover from component failures, transient network issues, and regional outages, thereby ensuring uninterrupted business continuity.

narratives.name: Reliability Core Purpose
narratives.description: The foundational philosophy of building highly resilient cloud applications.

narrativeContexts.context: Traditional on-premises infrastructure approaches rely heavily on redundant, high-end hardware to avoid failure entirely.

However, in hyperscale, distributed cloud environments, transient faults and hardware component failures are statistically inevitable and must be treated as standard operating conditions. The reliability practice shifts the engineering paradigm from an impossible goal of failure prevention to the practical reality of failure mitigation and rapid, automated recovery.

By implementing self-healing architectures, layered redundancy, and rigorous failure mode analysis, organizations can deliver high availability, protect critical business flows from extended downtime, and maintain customer trust during adverse events.

alphas.name: Reliability Targets
alphas.description: The quantitative metrics and qualitative goals defining the acceptable uptime, resiliency, and recovery thresholds for the workload.

narratives.name: Target Negotiation
narratives.description: The critical process of defining and negotiating reliability targets with stakeholders.

narrativeContexts.context: Establishing Reliability Targets involves negotiating Service Level Objectives (SLOs), Recovery Time Objectives (RTOs), and Recovery Point Objectives (RPOs) directly with business stakeholders based on the financial and reputational criticality of specific user flows.

Without clearly defined, measurable targets, engineering teams are forced to guess the business needs. This leads to either over-engineering solutions—wasting capital on unnecessary nines of availability—or under-engineering them, exposing the business to catastrophic revenue loss during outages.

This negotiation forces the business to confront the exponential cost curve associated with higher availability targets, facilitating informed trade-offs between architectural complexity, operational overhead, and business continuity.

states.name: Identified

checklist.name: Business Requirements Gathered

checklist.name: Critical Flows Listed

states.name: Tested

alphas.name: Resilient Architecture
alphas.description: The structural implementation of the workload, explicitly designed with redundancy and isolation to withstand and recover from faults.

narratives.name: Resilient Design Strategy
narratives.description: The technical approach to designing resilient cloud systems.

narrativeContexts.context: A resilient architecture assumes that components will fail and designs layers of redundancy to ensure overall system survival. This is the physical manifestation of the reliability targets.

Implementation requires separating critical path components, implementing active-active scale-out configurations, and utilizing self-healing platform features to minimize the blast radius of any single fault.

The architecture must incorporate graceful degradation, ensuring that if a non-critical microservice fails, the core transactional engine continues to serve users, albeit with reduced ancillary functionality.

states.name: Modeled

checklist.name: Redundancy Outlined

states.name: Designed
states.description: Detailed logical blueprints for fault isolation, active-active scaling, and self-preservation are complete (Maturity Level 2).

checklist.name: Redundancy Designed
checklist.description: Active-active or active-passive deployments are architected specifically for all critical flows.

checklist.name: Self-Preservation Mapped
checklist.description: Modular designs isolating faults, such as circuit breakers and bulkhead patterns, are logically mapped.

states.name: Implemented
states.description: Architecture is deployed with functional scaling and self-healing mechanisms active (Maturity Level 3).

checklist.name: Dynamic Scaling Active
checklist.description: Infrastructure is configured to dynamically scale based on load to prevent resource exhaustion failures.

checklist.name: Self-Healing Active
checklist.description: Built-in cloud patterns automatically replace failed stateless components and route traffic to healthy instances.

states.name: Proven
states.description: The architecture is fully automated, continuously validated, and self-remediating in production (Maturity Level 4).

checklist.name: Infrastructure as Code Deployed
checklist.description: The entire resilient architecture is deployed and maintained via declarative IaC artifacts.

checklist.name: Automated Remediation
checklist.description: Scripts and platform tools automatically remediate faults and trigger failovers without human intervention.

workProducts.name: Failure Mode Analysis
workProducts.description: A structured engineering assessment identifying potential dependencies, failure points, blast radiuses, and specific mitigation strategies.

narratives.name: FMA Value
narratives.description: The purpose and value of conducting a comprehensive Failure Mode Analysis.

narrativeContexts.context: To build true resiliency, teams must move beyond optimistic path engineering and systematically analyze every component to understand exactly what happens when it fails.
Optimistic path engineering leaves systems vulnerable to unknown, cascading failures during critical operations.

The Failure Mode Analysis provides the empirical blueprint for where to invest engineering hours in redundancy, circuit breakers, and automated recovery scripts, ensuring investments map directly to risk reduction.

narratives.name: Target Setting Process

narrativeContexts.context: The architect must engage business owners to determine the exact financial and reputational impact of downtime for specific user journeys. This shifts the conversation from abstract technical desires to concrete business risks.
However, technical desires must be grounded in reality and constrained by budgetary limits.
By translating technical trade-offs into financial metrics, the team can agree on realistic performance and recovery targets that justify the engineering effort required to achieve them.

practices.name: Security Practice
practices.description: This practice operationalizes the zero-trust model to ensure the absolute confidentiality, integrity, and availability of workloads. It dictates the methodology for systematic defense-in-depth strategies, identity management, and continuous threat mitigation.

narratives.name: Zero-Trust Posture
narratives.description: The strategic necessity of multi-layered security in highly distributed environments.

narrativeContexts.context: Cloud architectures inherently expand the attack surface exponentially compared to traditional, walled-garden on-premises networks. The perimeter is no longer physical; it is defined by identity and dynamic access policies.
Relying on traditional perimeter defense is insufficient, leaving internal data exposed to lateral movement.

By enforcing a zero-trust model—verifying explicitly at every boundary, using strict least-privilege access, and engineering under the assumption of breach—organizations protect data integrity and maintain regulatory compliance.

checklist.name: Perimeters Defined

practices.name: Cost Optimization Practice

narratives.name: Cloud Economics
narratives.description: The mechanisms to prevent cloud waste and align technical spend with business utility.

narrativeContexts.context: Cloud computing replaces traditional, predictable capital expenditure with highly variable operational expenditure. This enables vast scalability but introduces the severe risk of runaway costs and unmonitored resource sprawl.
Reactive cost-cutting often damages business agility and system performance.

True Cost Optimization requires a proactive discipline of establishing precise spending guardrails, aligning usage to underlying billing increments, and mathematically right-sizing environments to ensure every dollar deployed yields measurable business value.

practices.name: Operational Excellence Practice

narratives.name: DevOps and Observability
narratives.description: The necessity of standardized workflows, rigorous automation, and cultural alignment.

narrativeContexts.context: To maintain high workload quality at velocity, traditional silos between engineering and operations teams must be dismantled. Organizations must embrace a shared responsibility model where developers own the operational health of their code.
Without rigorous automation, manual human intervention introduces catastrophic risk and limits deployment frequency.

Operational Excellence dictates the relentless automation of repetitive tasks. By utilizing Infrastructure as Code (IaC) and robust CI/CD pipelines, teams guarantee safe, incremental, and highly predictable deployments, severely limiting the blast radius of human error.
